item.title: FHTA says tourism tax backlash was avoidable
item.description: The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association says the growing backlash over the new Tourism Services Tax in Fiji’s key visitor markets was “entirely avoidable”, claiming Government was warned months ago about problems with its implementation. FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said the association raised concerns as soon as the five per cent levy was announced and proposed alternatives tha
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association says the growing backlash over the new Tourism Services Tax in Fiji’s key visitor markets was “entirely avoidable”, claiming Government was warned months ago about problems with its implementation.

FHTA chief executive officer Fantasha Lockington said the association raised concerns as soon as the five per cent levy was announced and proposed alternatives that would provide direct support to Fiji Airways without imposing a broader tax across the tourism supply chain.

“We tried to make this work from day one, and we were ignored at every turn,” Ms Lockington said.

“We asked that pre-booked and paid holidays be exempted, the same treatment given under the old Service Turnover Tax. We asked for clarity on the sunset clause. Both requests were left out of the final Gazette, without explanation.”

FHTA said it also requested at least four weeks between the release of the Fiji Revenue and Customs Service’s Standard Interpretation Guidelines and implementation of the tax.

However, it said the guidelines were only finalised yesterday — 10 days before the tax takes effect on September 1.

“We handed government a clear, specific warning of exactly how complicated this was going to be to administer,” Ms Lockington said.

“That warning was not heard, or it was heard and dismissed. Either way, the result is the mess our travel partners are now scrambling to clean up, with days rather than weeks to do it.”

The criticism comes as travel industry groups in Australia and New Zealand raise concerns about the treatment of existing bookings.

FHTA said travel agents handling multi-resort itineraries were facing difficulties because of uncertainty around collection arrangements, including the need to re-invoice wholesalers and customers for bookings settled months earlier.

Ms Lockington said Fiji’s tourism industry had invested significant time and resources into establishing the country as a credible and well-run destination.

“That reputation is being damaged this week, not because of the tax itself, but because government would not listen when we told them exactly how to avoid this outcome,” she said.

FHTA said travel agents, wholesalers and tour operators now had little more than a week to adjust booking systems, invoicing processes and customer communications.

Ms Lockington also linked the debate to Fiji Airways’ wider financial position, noting Parliament had approved a further $200 million Government guarantee for the airline’s borrowing on August 17.

“Our industry is not against Fiji investing in its own aviation sector. What we needed was consultation, time and clarity, and we asked for all three, repeatedly, well before this became a crisis,” she said.

“Government had every opportunity to get this right. It chose not to take it.”

item.title: Police clearance applications generate $4.3M in 2025
item.description: The Fiji Police Force processed 52,694 police clearance applications last year, generating $4.3 million in revenue, Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua told Parliament on Friday. Mr Naivalurua said demand for Police Clearance Certificates had increased significantly, with 8,482 more applications processed compared with 2024.
item.content:encoded:
The Fiji Police Force processed 52,694 police clearance applications last year, generating $4.3 million in revenue, Minister for Policing Ioane Naivalurua told Parliament on Friday.

Mr Naivalurua said demand for Police Clearance Certificates had increased significantly, with 8,482 more applications processed compared with 2024.

“Mr Speaker, Sir, in 2024, the Fiji Police Force processed a total of 44,212 applications with a total revenue earning of $3.8 million,” he said.

“Last year, these numbers increased by 8,482. A total of 52,694 applications were successfully processed, generating a total earning of $4.3 million.”

Mr Naivalurua said a Police Clearance Certificate was an official document confirming whether an applicant had a criminal record in Fiji.

“This is a requirement for employment, visa, residency applications, study abroad, to name a few,” he said.

He also outlined the application process, saying forms were available from the Police Clearance Office at the Fiji Police Force Headquarters in Suva, selected police stations and the Force’s official website.

Applicants are required to complete the prescribed form and provide supporting documents, which may include a recent passport-sized photograph, a certified copy of valid photo identification and proof of address.

Fingerprints may also be required in some cases.

Mr Naivalurua said applicants must pay the prescribed fee at designated Police revenue collection offices and should retain their receipts for tracking and follow-up purposes.

“Once the clearance is processed, it will only be emailed and posted to the relevant organisation or agency that requested a police clearance,” he said.

He said applicants wanting to check the status of their applications should use the telephone numbers and email addresses provided on the Fiji Police Force’s official website or call 9905201.

Mr Naivalurua also clarified that follow-up enquiries should “not [be made] to the Commissioner.”

For people seeking Fiji police clearance from overseas, he said application forms could be accessed through the Fiji Police Force website or obtained from the nearest Fiji High Commission, embassy or consulate.

item.title: Usamate, Turaga clash in Parliament over Legal Aid assistance
item.description: A heated exchange erupted in Parliament between MP Jone Usamate and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga over the $15,000 income threshold for Legal Aid assistance, with Speaker Filimone Jitoko intervening during the debate on Friday. Mr Usamate had sought clarity on how eligibility was determined when the $15,000 threshold was not strictly applied and what criteria were used to assess applicatio
item.content:encoded:
A heated exchange erupted in Parliament between MP Jone Usamate and Acting Attorney-General Siromi Turaga over the $15,000 income threshold for Legal Aid assistance, with Speaker Filimone Jitoko intervening during the debate on Friday.

Mr Usamate had sought clarity on how eligibility was determined when the $15,000 threshold was not strictly applied and what criteria were used to assess applications on merit.

“I think the question was very simple and required a simple answer and we had this meandering. Very poor!” Mr Usamate said.

He questioned whether standard criteria could be provided while a review of the system was being undertaken.

“What does merit mean? So that people can really understand whether they are eligible for getting Legal Aid Commission assistance or not,” he said.

Mr Turaga responded by criticising the former government.

“That was a government that sat there for 16 years and did nothing. They have a memory lapse. You did nothing. Your Minister did nothing,” he said.

Mr Usamate immediately raised a point of order, initially accusing the Minister of “lying”, before the Speaker instructed him to withdraw the word.

“The honourable Minister is misleading the House, Sir,” Mr Usamate responded.

He argued that the former government had expanded Legal Aid services around the country and introduced the threshold.

“The former Government took the Legal Aid Commission to every corner of this country. That is not nothing. Nothing means zilch, nada, zero.”

The Speaker acknowledged Mr Usamate’s point.

“Even if they had gone around consulting without actually bringing any change, they were doing something. You know what I mean. Technically, he is correct,” the Speaker said.

Mr Turaga maintained that the income threshold had not been changed despite changing social and economic conditions.

He said expanding eligibility also carried significant financial implications.

“We cannot grow Legal Aid,” Mr Turaga said.

“Legal Aid is probably the largest law firm, and they are trying their level best to handle the workload. There is also a budgetary constraint.”

Mr Turaga said the Director of Legal Aid retained discretion over assistance and that a review had been directed to ensure eligible people could access Legal Aid services.

“A review has been directed to ensure that people who are entitled to Legal Aid will be assisted,” he said.

item.title: Money for Prados, but not for teachers – Seruiratu slams government
item.description: Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned the Government’s spending priorities, claiming it can find money for Toyota Land Cruiser Prados and government vehicles while salary upgrades for hundreds of teachers remain dependent on available funding. His criticism follows Education Minister Aseri Radrodro’s confirmation that 410 teachers applied for salary upgrades between August 1, 2025 and Ju
item.content:encoded:
Opposition Leader Inia Seruiratu has questioned the Government’s spending priorities, claiming it can find money for Toyota Land Cruiser Prados and government vehicles while salary upgrades for hundreds of teachers remain dependent on available funding.

His criticism follows Education Minister Aseri Radrodro’s confirmation that 410 teachers applied for salary upgrades between August 1, 2025 and June 30, 2026 after attaining and submitting upgraded qualifications.

However, only 273 applications have been identified for processing during the 2026-2027 financial year, and those remain “subject to the availability and release of the required funding”.

Mr Seruiratu questioned why certainty could not be provided to teachers who had invested time and money in improving their qualifications.

“I refuse to accept the excuse that Government simply does not have enough resources,” he said.

“This Government always seems to find money when it suits its own priorities.”

Mr Seruiratu specifically pointed to spending on government vehicles and what he described as an unnecessarily large Cabinet.

“It has found the resources to maintain an unnecessarily large ministerial cabinet. It can have Ministers alongside Permanent Secretaries across ministries. It can find money for Government vehicles and the latest Toyota Land Cruiser Prados,” he said.

“But when 410 teachers come forward after upgrading their qualifications, suddenly we are talking about the ‘availability and release of the required funding’.”

Mr Seruiratu said the response raised questions about what would happen to the 137 applicants who have not been identified for processing this financial year.

He also questioned what guarantee existed for the 273 applications earmarked for processing when their upgrades remained dependent on funding.

“That tells the public everything they need to know about the priorities of this Government,” he said.

“When it comes to itself, Government finds the money. When it comes to teachers, teachers are pushed to the back of the line.”

Mr Seruiratu said teachers had sacrificed their time and, in many cases, their own money to obtain higher qualifications and should be rewarded for improving their skills.

The Education Minister’s parliamentary response did not address Mr Seruiratu’s subsequent criticism concerning government vehicles or Land Cruiser Prados.

item.title: ‘Money wasted’: Chief Justice criticises COI legal advice
item.description: CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has criticised the legal advice given to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu over the extension of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC commissioner Barbara Malimali, saying lawyers had failed to properly examine the limits of the President’s powers. Justice Temo made the comments while addressing newly admitted lawyers, using the inquiry as an exa
item.content:encoded:
CHIEF Justice Salesi Temo has criticised the legal advice given to President Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu over the extension of the Commission of Inquiry into the appointment of former FICAC commissioner Barbara Malimali, saying lawyers had failed to properly examine the limits of the President’s powers.

Justice Temo made the comments while addressing newly admitted lawyers, using the inquiry as an example of the importance of providing accurate legal advice and understanding the limits imposed by legislation.

He described the outcome as “money wasted”, saying the responsibility lay with the lawyers rather than the clients who relied on their advice.

“We’ve got to work and find out what are the parameters of your power to continue with that legal work,” Justice Temo said.

He referred to the High Court judgment of Justice Dane Tuiqereqere, which found that the President did not have the power under the Commission of Inquiry Act to extend the inquiry beyond the statutory period.

“Lawyers were hired from overseas and they didn’t read the COI Act properly to show that His Excellency the President doesn’t have the power to extend it.

“As a result, all the work that they did later was pronounced ultra vires and null and void.”

The Chief Justice said the failure to identify the legal limitation resulted in the commission continuing its hearings without valid legal authority, adding that the matter demonstrated the responsibility lawyers had to examine legislation carefully and determine the limits of their clients’ legal powers.

“That is your work as lawyers, to dig, dig, dig. Obviously, the lawyer involved in that (advising the President) was amiss, (and) didn’t find it.

When approached by The Fiji Times separately about the same High Court judgment that raised concerns of the appropriateness of Ms Malimali’s appointment, the Chief Justice declined to comment and directed questions to Justice Dane Tuiqereqere who delivered the judgment.

Justice Temo is the chairman of the Judicial Service Commission, which handled key judicial appointments, including the position of FiCAC Commissioner.

While ruling the findings of the COI null and void after finding the inquiry was tainted by bias and breached the rules of natural justice, Justice Tuiqereqere said it had served its purpose. He said Ms Malimali was not appropriate for the post in light of an active criminal investigation and an incident in Tuvalu.

item.title: Fire destroys Drasa grower’s farm
item.description: DRASA sector grower Nilesh Prasad lost 90 per cent of his farm to an uncontrollable fire that claimed close to 100 tonnes of sugar cane and $3000 worth of pineapple. Mr Prasad said their attempts to put out the fire last Wednesday was futile because of the dry conditions.
item.content:encoded:
DRASA sector grower Nilesh Prasad lost 90 per cent of his farm to an uncontrollable fire that claimed close to 100 tonnes of sugar cane and $3000 worth of pineapple.

Mr Prasad said their attempts to put out the fire last Wednesday was futile because of the dry conditions.

“We don’t usually get this kind of fire that spread so quickly,” said Mr Prasad. “It started from one very small end of the cane field, and it quickly spread to the other sections.

“The fire started around 3pm and it took about three hours for us to control it.” He said the dry conditions had made it worse.

“It’s been very dry. So when a fire starts, it spreads very quickly.”

Mr Prasad’s farm and many others located within the Western Division had fallen victim to indiscriminate burning. Sugar Cane Growers Council CEO Vimal Dutt said stakeholders had been briefed about the prolonged dry spell they anticipate would also impact the sugar industry.

“We are expecting issues of farms burning, water supply going low and food security concerns,” he said.

“So we are doing our best to implement some immediate and long term measures for our growers.”

Nilesh Prasad (middle) with his labourers at his farm in Drasa, Lautoka. Picture: REINAL CHAND

item.title: Grey listing risk
item.description: FIJI could face serious economic consequences, including possible grey listing, if it fails an international assessment of its anti-money laundering and financial crime measures next month. Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament Fiji’s money laundering risk remained high, with drug offences, organised crime, tax and customs crimes, illegal fishing, bribery and corruption identified among t
item.content:encoded:
FIJI could face serious economic consequences, including possible grey listing, if it fails an international assessment of its anti-money laundering and financial crime measures next month.

Justice Minister Siromi Turaga told Parliament Fiji’s money laundering risk remained high, with drug offences, organised crime, tax and customs crimes, illegal fishing, bribery and corruption identified among the key threats.

“It is important that Fiji does well in the mutual evaluation,” Mr Turaga said.

He warned that an unfavourable outcome could result in grey listing by international partners and financial institutions.

The Asia Pacific Group on money laundering assessment will examine Fiji’s legal framework as well as how effectively authorities investigate and prosecute financial crimes, use financial intelligence and confiscate criminal assets.

An assessment team is expected in Fiji in September for discussions and interviews with Government and private sector representatives.

Mr Turaga said Fiji had made significant progress since its previous assessment in 2015, including the establishment of a dedicated civil forfeiture unit within the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said forfeiture cases had increased, with the biggest recent case involving almost $9million in properties.

Active cases currently involve about $11m in assets, most linked to drug-related cases.

Mr Turaga said the assessment outcome would influence decisions by institutions including the IMF, World Bank and international banks on investment, financing and trade with Fiji.

item.title: AOG Fiji breaks ground for new HQ
item.description: The Assemblies of God of Fiji has begun construction of a new $17.9million seven-storey headquarters in Suva, with church leaders describing the project as the fulfilment of a vision developed over several years. Reverend Filikesa Koroivueta said the project was driven by the church’s general superintendent Reverend Moses Cakau, who took up the vision with “zeal and passion” about two to three yea
item.content:encoded:
The Assemblies of God of Fiji has begun construction of a new $17.9million seven-storey headquarters in Suva, with church leaders describing the project as the fulfilment of a vision developed over several years.

Reverend Filikesa Koroivueta said the project was driven by the church’s general superintendent Reverend Moses Cakau, who took up the vision with “zeal and passion” about two to three years ago.

He said the building would become a landmark in Suva and provide members with a sense of pride and belonging. The project was first developed in 2021 with construction expected to take 15 months and will use prefabricated materials.

The church also plans to develop its Bible School on iTaukei land and utilise vacant land in Koronivia provided by the Ministry of Lands, with part of the property earmarked for commercial development to support its ministries and schools.
